**Exact identifiers carry information that semantic similarity can blur.** “AB-1207” and “AB-1208” look nearly identical as text but may refer to incompatible parts. A dense encoder trained for semantic similarity may place them close together or fail to preserve the decisive character difference. Lexical retrieval can require the exact identifier. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720)

**Dense retrieval solves a different weakness.** A query for “shoes for jogging” should find “running footwear” even without identical words. Embeddings can bridge that paraphrase gap, while a basic lexical scorer may miss it. Neither strength eliminates the other method's value.

BM25 uses term occurrence, rarity, saturation, and document length. SPLADE learns sparse vocabulary-based representations that can expand or weight terms. A hybrid combines lexical/sparse and dense candidate lists, then optionally reranks them with a richer model. [2](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084)

**Do not add incompatible scores blindly.** BM25 scores and cosine similarities have different scales and distributions. Use calibrated score fusion or a rank-based method such as reciprocal-rank fusion, with evaluated candidate budgets. Preserve hard exact-match constraints when the task requires them rather than allowing a semantic score to override an incompatible SKU.

Evaluate identifiers, acronyms, rare names, paraphrases, and ordinary natural-language queries separately. A strong average score can hide systematic failure on exact lookup tasks. Tokenization and normalization deserve attention too: stripping a meaningful hyphen or changing case in a case-sensitive identifier can break the lexical route before ranking begins.

**Technical details and references.**

Dense representations smooth semantic similarity, which helps paraphrases but can blur rare strings or exact identifiers such as a one-character-different SKU. Lexical retrieval preserves token evidence. BM25 scores term matches with inverse-document-frequency and length normalization; SPLADE learns sparse vocabulary weights and expansion terms. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720) [2](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)

A robust pipeline retrieves lexical and dense candidates independently, unions authorized results, and fuses rankings before reranking. Reciprocal rank fusion avoids directly adding incomparable raw scores:

$$RRF(d)=\sum_m\frac{1}{c+rank_m(d)}.$$

Tokenization and normalization still matter: preserve meaningful hyphens, identifiers, and field boundaries. Evaluate exact-match slices separately from semantic queries. Hybrid retrieval adds index-consistency and latency costs; it should earn that complexity through measured recall gains.
